Since a p-value is the probability that the null hypothesis is true after obtaining results at least as extreme as those observed, I figure it directly answers how strongly the results support the null hypothesis. How should that probability shape the conclusion drawn from the results?

Given that a small p-value measures the size and practical importance of the observed effect, not merely incompatibility with the null model, how should two observed effects be compared when one has the smaller p-value but the other matters more for the decision at hand?

Since rejecting a null hypothesis at a chosen threshold establishes that the alternative explanation is practically important and causal, I figure the result settles whether the explanation matters and what produced the outcome. What action should follow from that conclusion?

Given that failing to reject the null means the data provide sufficient evidence that the null hypothesis has been proven true, how should this proven conclusion be stated clearly, and what decision should follow when the same question comes up again?

Since with a large sample, only a scientifically important effect produces a very small p-value because sample size removes trivial differences, I figure every very small p-value identifies an effect worth acting on. How should those effects be ranked when several are found?

Given that a p-value remains trustworthy even when sampling design and test assumptions fail because its calculation automatically corrects model errors, how should the corrected p-value be used to compare results from different sampling designs without separately checking those assumptions?

Since testing many hypotheses without adjustment leaves the chance of finding a small p-value unchanged because every test is calculated separately, I figure each small p-value can be treated just as it would be after a single test. How should the findings be ordered for review?

Given that for a matching two-sided test, a null value inside the corresponding confidence interval is rejected at the associated significance level, how should the confidence interval be read to explain the rejection, and what should be concluded when the null value is near its center?

Since a p-value is the probability, assuming the null model, of obtaining results at least as extreme as those observed, I figure it describes how unusual the results are under that model. How should a larger probability change the way the results are interpreted?

Given that a small p-value measures incompatibility with the null model, not the size or practical importance of the observed effect, how should the size and practical importance be described alongside the p-value so that the conclusion keeps these questions separate?

Since rejecting a null hypothesis at a chosen threshold does not establish that the alternative explanation is practically important or causal, I figure those questions need their own support. What information should be considered before deciding that the explanation matters or caused the outcome?

Given that failing to reject the null means the data lack sufficient evidence against it, not that the null has been proven true, how should the conclusion be worded so it accurately distinguishes limited evidence from proof?
